title: Nonconvex-strongly-concave problems without control of dual initialization

description_paragraphs:
$$
\min_{x\in\mathbb{R}^{d_x}}\Phi(x),\qquad\Phi(x)=\max_{y\in\mathbb{R}^{d_y}}f(x,y).
$$

assumptions.description:
On the declared function domain, $\|
abla f(z)-
abla f(w)\|\le eta\|z-w\|$. The vector $
abla f$ includes both blocks $x,y$.
For each fixed $x$, $-f(x,\cdot)$ is $\mu_y$-strongly convex, uniformly in $x$.

assumptions.scope: Public initial point; the objective-gap or distance term refers to the same solution or value function explicitly specified in this entry

assumptions.description: Neither $x\mapsto f(x,y)$ nor the optimal-value function $\Phi$ is additionally assumed convex.

model.parameter_domain_description: $\Delta$: positive real; $\beta$: positive real; $d$: integer at least 2; $\varepsilon$: positive real; $\mu_y$: $0<\mu_y\le\beta$. Derived quantities are defined in the parameter table. Each region states any additional accuracy and dimension conditions.
description_paragraphs: $f:\mathbb{R}^{d_x}\times\mathbb{R}^{d_y}\to\mathbb{R}$, with both blocks unconstrained and Euclidean norms throughout. The joint gradient satisfies $\|\nabla f(z)-\nabla f(w)\|_2\le \beta\|z-w\|_2$.

For every $x$, $f(x,\cdot)$ is uniformly $\mu_y$-strongly concave. Thus $y^\star(x)=\arg\max_y f(x,y)$ is unique and $\Phi(x)=f(x,y^\star(x))$ is differentiable. Neither $f(\cdot,y)$ nor $\Phi$ is assumed convex.
Assume $\inf_x\Phi(x)>-\infty$, with an initial point satisfying $\Phi(x_0)-\inf_x\Phi(x)\le\Delta$.
The initial point $(x_0,y_0)=(0,0)$ is public. There is no uniform upper bound on $\|\nabla_y f(0,0)\|_2$, $\|y_0-y^\star(x_0)\|_2$, or the dual gap.

The dimension $d_x,d_y$ is a finite positive integer visible to the algorithm. Complexity takes a uniform worst case over these dimensions. Candidate budgets may not depend on the hidden instance’s dual-initialization scale.

operations.order_convention: Derivative order refers to the scalar payoff $f$. The joint gradient has two blocks; the response signature specifies whether a Hessian or complete derivative jet is supplied.

feedback_quality.description: Exact responses from the same hidden object fixed before interaction

operations.coupling: Deterministic exact responses with repeated queries allowed; stochastic sample-reuse permissions are irrelevant.

public_inputs: Public inputs include block dimensions $d_x,d_y$ and $\Delta$, $\beta$, $\varepsilon$, and $\mu_y$, together with the stated initial-point and feasible-domain information. Analytic representations of hidden functions, operators, or matrices are not revealed.
description_paragraphs: Public inputs include block dimensions $d_x,d_y$ and $\Delta$, $\beta$, $\varepsilon$, and $\mu_y$, together with the stated initial-point and feasible-domain information. Analytic representations of hidden functions, operators, or matrices are not revealed.

$$
(x,y)\in\mathbb{R}^{d_x+d_y}\longmapsto (\nabla_x f(x,y),\nabla_y f(x,y))
$$
Responses are exact and noiseless; neither function values nor Hessians are returned.
The interface does not directly supply $y^\star(x)$, $\Phi(x)$, or $\nabla\Phi(x)$. Every primitive gradient used for inner optimization is charged.

output.feasibility: Return only the primal block $\widehat x\in X$. An optimal inner point is not required.
output.allowed_postprocessing: arbitrary measurable postprocessing; unqueried output permitted unless restriction says otherwise
description_paragraphs: Return a single $\widehat x\in\mathbb R^{d_x}$. No dual point is required.

The output may be any measurable postprocessing of the history, including an unqueried point, average, or convex combination. It must satisfy the stated domain and feasibility requirements; no additional function value or computable certificate is required.

metric.normalization: exactly as displayed; no square/norm interchange
metric.finiteness_conditions: compact domain and continuous data, or the specific coercivity/existence promise stated in MODEL
description_paragraphs:
$$
\|\nabla\Phi(\widehat{x})\|_2
$$
The identity $\nabla\Phi(x)=\nabla_xf(x,y^\star(x))$ specifies the evaluation target and does not supply an additional information interface.

description_paragraphs: One full joint gradient costs one $N_{\mathrm{grad}}$ call. Both blocks are returned together, not charged as two calls.
Use a fixed worst-case budget: calls never exceed the prespecified $N$ on any instance or random execution path. Earlier stopping within the budget is permitted.

Here $+\infty$ means that for every finite candidate budget $N$, some finite dimension and admissible instance prevent any $N$-call algorithm from achieving success probability $2/3$. It does not assert that every fixed finite-dimensional instance is unsolvable or requires infinitely many calls.

Count all information calls for one instance and one requested accuracy, including initialization. Exact-real arithmetic, storage, and solving known models from public inputs and returned data are uncharged. This query-complexity quantity does not certify arithmetic or bit complexity.

objects.definition: Unknown real-valued payoff function $f:\mathbb R^{d_x}\times\mathbb R^{d_y}\to\mathbb R$.
$\Phi(x)=\max_{y\in\mathbb R^{d_y}}f(x,y)$. Strong concavity gives a unique inner optimizer $y^*(x)$, but neither its location nor its value is supplied for free by the oracle.

norms.definition: The Euclidean norm and inner product are $\|v\|_2=(\sum_jv_j^2)^{1/2}$ and $\langle u,v\rangle=\sum_j u_jv_j$. On the joint space use $\|(x,y)\|_2=(\|x\|_2^2+\|y\|_2^2)^{1/2}$.

quantities.analysis_scope: The algorithm may read the finite block dimensions. A single algorithm family must succeed with probability at least $2/3$ on every admissible instance, with a budget uniform over all finite dimensions. If no successful algorithm family or uniform finite budget exists, the complexity is $+\infty$.

bounds.method: Two-ended dual chain with exact gradients: independent fair signs and a random orthogonal frame

bounds.algorithm_class_scope: Any measurable adaptive randomized queries and measurable final primal output are allowed. Query vectors may be dense, nonlinear, and unbounded in norm. The fixed budget applies to every execution path.

conditions: The noiseless hard instances in Theorem 3.6 already belong to this exact joint-gradient model. Neither stochastic oracle noise nor a linear-span restriction is needed.

The hard distribution in Appendix B is fixed before interaction and independent of the algorithmic seed. At every finite budget $N$, average success probability is at most $7/12$. Hence some fixed admissible instance has success probability below $2/3$.
applicability.dimension_conditions: For each $N\ge1$, choose $d_x=1$ and chain length $m=4N+4$. Equation (20) of Theorem B.2 supplies a sufficiently large finite $d_y$. Both $d_y$ and initial dual residual may grow with $N$. Infinite complexity at fixed $d_y$ is not proved.
applicability.oracle_mapping: Each call returns both gradient blocks exactly. The source hard construction supplies no function values, Hessians, inner solutions, or reduced gradients, matching this interface exactly.
applicability.guarantee_mapping: The success event is $\|\nabla\Phi(\widehat x)\|_2\le\varepsilon$, with probability over the algorithmic seed only. A distribution-average success upper bound establishes failure on at least one fixed instance.
applicability.output_mapping: The successful primal-output intervals for the two hidden signs are disjoint. The output argument in Theorem B.2 allows unqueried points of arbitrary norm.
applicability.resource_mapping: A uniform finite integer N bounds all joint-gradient calls on every instance and every execution path. It is not a worst-instance expected stopping time.
